title: Frontier Language Models Struggle to Copy: Text Can Be Better Viewed in 2D
hook: LLMs can solve hard reasoning problems in seconds but fumble at exactly copying text in their own context. The culprit: positional encodings biased toward shortcuts, fixed by laying text out in 2D.
key_points: Even frontier LLMs fail to exactly copy an input string that fits comfortably in their context window.
Cause: standard positional encodings bias models toward copying via local-context matching instead of precise position lookup.
2D-RoPE arranges text as a grid, giving each token a row and column ID, so copying becomes a fixed column-offset lookup.
Shallow Transformers with 2D-RoPE copy perfectly at input lengths hundreds of times longer than their training lengths.
The copying advantage holds up in large-scale pretraining on DCLM at model sizes up to 1.4B parameters.
content_html: It's a strange failure mode: an LLM can chain together multi-step reasoning in seconds, yet asked to exactly reproduce a string that's sitting right there in its context, it slips up. This paper traces that failure to something structural — how Transformers encode position.
extra_html:
Haodong Wen, Kaifeng Lyu, and colleagues argue standard positional encodings give Transformers an inductive bias toward copying via a shortcut: matching local context patterns rather than precisely locating the corresponding position in the input. Their fix, 2D-RoPE, lays text out on a 2D grid instead of a 1D sequence, assigning each token a row ID and a column ID. Under that view, copying becomes simply reading off tokens at a fixed column offset — a far easier pattern to learn than tracking absolute 1D position.

In synthetic copy experiments, shallow Transformers using 2D-RoPE achieve perfect copying at input lengths hundreds of times longer than anything seen in training, while standard positional encodings fall far behind. The advantage isn't just a synthetic-task artifact either: it persists in large-scale pretraining on the DCLM dataset at model sizes up to 1.4B parameters. The authors frame this as a broader case for exploring 2D positional encodings in language modeling. arXiv, July 2026.

related.title: RoPE: Rotary Position Embedding
related.hook: Encode position by rotating query/key vectors - relative distances then fall out of the dot product for free, no extra tokens or additive embeddings needed.

flashcards.prompt: What surprising failure do frontier LLMs show, per this paper?
flashcards.back_html: They fail to exactly copy an input string even when it fits well within their context window — a much simpler task than the reasoning problems they can solve.

flashcards.prompt: Why do the authors say this copying failure happens?

choices.text: Positional encodings bias the model toward a local-context-matching shortcut instead of precise position lookup
The model's vocabulary is too small to represent rare tokens
Copying requires more parameters than reasoning does

flashcards.explanation_html: They attribute it to Transformer positional encodings whose inductive bias favors matching local context over locating the exact corresponding input position.

flashcards.prompt: How does 2D-RoPE change what 'copying' means for the model?
flashcards.back_html: It gives each token a row and column ID on a 2D grid, so copying reduces to retrieving tokens at a fixed column offset — an easy pattern to learn.

flashcards.prompt: How well did 2D-RoPE generalize to longer inputs than seen in training?

choices.text: Shallow Transformers achieved perfect copying at input lengths hundreds of times longer than training length
It matched standard RoPE exactly, with no extrapolation advantage
It only worked up to 2x the training length

flashcards.explanation_html: In synthetic experiments, 2D-RoPE models copied perfectly at lengths hundreds of times beyond training, far outperforming standard positional encodings.
